newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - BBC World Service extends lifeline to Africa.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - BBC World Service extends lifeline to Africa.

text.p: For many refugees who lost their homes and families during the crises in Rwanda and Zaire, a daily BBC broadcast provides a lifeline to the outside world and to their lost relatives.
Refugees crowd round radio sets in the evening waiting for "Gahuzamiryango" to come on air. Some are hoping they will hear the voices of their lost children over the airwaves.

"Every evening, when the time of Gahuzamiryango arrives, you can see groups of refugees ranging from 10 to 100 listening to Gahuzamiryango. They say it is their only source of reliable information and the only place they can hear their messages," said Shinani Kabendera, a journalist in Tanzania.
The only criticism was that the World Service programme was too short.
So, on December 9, the BBC doubled the length of the programme to 30 minutes, broadcasting messages to and from refugees but also providing news on the situation in Rwanda and Zaire.
The programme was named Gahuzamiryango, meaning "helping put families back together". It is also the nickname for a Rwandan beer.

"With many (refugees) still in Tanzania and Zaire, and the whole situation continually changing there is a tremendous thirst for news and humanitarian assistance," said Benny Ammar, BBC Regional Head, Africa and the Middle East.
NEWS, PLAYS, SPORT IN LONGER PROGRAMME
Interviews with doctors and healthworkers, short plays, readings of traditional Kiyarwanda/Kirundi legends, international news and sports coverage will be included in the expanded broadcasts.

"We're going to do more educational slots particularly concentrating on health, for example diarrhoea, malaria and AIDS, and also how to deal with children suffering from trauma," said Kari Blackburn, head of the BBC World Service Swahili service and coordinator of the Great Lakes Lifeline Service.
The Great Lakes region includes western Uganda, western Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire. But messages from children separated from their families remain at the core of the programme.

The first extended broadcast went out at 1815 local time (1615 GMT) on December 9. It included an extended news broadcast, listeners' letters, messages from refugees and sports reports from Rwanda including basketball and cycling.
"We didn't want it all to be doom and gloom...there's this tremendous audience and in a way we wanted to give them something to make them feel normal as well," Blackburn said.
BRITISH AID MINISTRY PROVIDES FUNDS

The Great Lakes service received no money from the BBC World Service itself after the initial project grant of 30,000 pounds ($49,720), relying instead on funding from the Overseas Development Administration (Britain's aid ministry) and five non-governmental organisations (NGOs).
The UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) has provided additional funding for the extended broadcasts.
"We consider it vital that the refugees have an alternative source of information about conditions of return inside Rwanda to that which is circulated in the camps," it said.
The programme is broadcast in a mixture of the Kinyarwanda and Kirundi languages, which are mutually understandable and are spoken by an estimated 80 percent of Rwandans and Burundians.

It was originally launched as a temporary "lifeline" service in September 1994, in conjunction with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and other organisations seeking to reunite those separated by war.
The programme now has three full-time producers, two Burundians and one Rwandan, and two part-time producers and is broadcast from London.
It also has a network of five regular freelance journalists in the region, as well as access to reports from BBC staff correspondents.

"Because our programme doesn't come from any one particular source and because it covers the region on a wider basis it is trusted and listened to," Blackburn said, adding they were careful to have no political agenda.
Research by the UNHCR showed that, despite the brevity of the BBC broadcasts, the World Service was the most popular and most listened to radio station across the region.

"We want to continue it (the programme) for as long as the crisis in the Great Lakes region continues. We've got definite funding till March '97 and positive indications of funding for a further year, but nothing absolutely definite," Blackburn said.
